questions.q: What is the actual difference between an X-Ray segment and a subsegment?
options: A subsegment covers multiple services while a segment covers only one function call
A segment is the record of one service's work on a request; a subsegment is a finer breakdown within it, such as one downstream call
They are identical in meaning — X-Ray uses the two terms interchangeably in its API
A segment only exists for Lambda functions, while a subsegment only exists for EC2-hosted services
questions.explain: A segment records one service's overall work on a request (start/end time, metadata); a subsegment nests inside it to break that work down further, such as one call out to DynamoDB or a downstream service.

questions.q: Why does the X-Ray SDK send completed segment data to the local X-Ray daemon over UDP instead of calling the X-Ray API directly from application code?
options: UDP is required because the X-Ray API only accepts binary-encoded requests
The X-Ray daemon encrypts trace data before it can leave the account, which the SDK cannot do on its own
Application code is not permitted to make any outbound network calls under AWS IAM by default
It keeps the latency and batching work of actually reaching the X-Ray API off the request path that's being measured, instead of adding tracing overhead to the thing being traced
questions.explain: The daemon runs as a separate background process (sidecar, DaemonSet, or built into the Lambda execution environment) that batches and forwards trace data, so instrumenting a request doesn't itself add API-call latency to that request.

questions.q: How does X-Ray build a service map, and what is it useful for on a real incident?
options: It's assembled automatically from segment data showing which services called which downstream services, and it's useful for quickly spotting which node in the chain is actually degraded
It must be hand-drawn by an engineer in the X-Ray console before any traces can be collected
It's a static architecture diagram uploaded once during initial X-Ray setup and never updated
It only shows AWS Lambda functions and omits any EC2, ECS, or container-based services entirely
questions.explain: Because every segment records its own service and its downstream calls, X-Ray can build the topology graph automatically — and a node showing elevated errors or latency is often the fastest way to localize a problem before opening individual traces.

questions.q: What does a sampling rule's `reservoir_size` actually guarantee?
options: The maximum number of segments that can ever be stored for that service, after which tracing stops entirely
The number of days trace data for that service is retained before automatic deletion
A fixed number of traces per second that are always traced before the fixed_rate percentage sampling applies to anything beyond that
The number of subsegments allowed inside a single segment for that service
questions.explain: The reservoir is a guaranteed baseline — e.g. 2 traces per second always traced — with the fixed_rate percentage only applying to request volume beyond that reserved amount, ensuring low-traffic or critical paths aren't sampled away to nothing.

questions.q: Why would you set a near-zero sampling rate specifically on a health-check endpoint like /health?
options: Health-check endpoints are automatically excluded by AWS and the sampling rule has no real effect
Health checks produce traces that tell you almost nothing interesting during an incident, so tracing nearly every one of them wastes storage and API calls on noise
X-Ray refuses to trace any endpoint that returns a 200 status code without an error
A near-zero rate on health checks is required before any other service's sampling rule can take effect
questions.explain: Frequent, low-value health-check traffic generates a large volume of traces that tell you nothing useful on an incident, so a custom sampling rule with a very low fixed_rate (or zero reservoir) keeps that noise from crowding out traces you'd actually want to look at.
